name: Carta
tagline: Cap table, equity issuance, 409A valuations and fund administration for startups and their investors.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The spreadsheet part of Carta is genuinely easy: share classes, issuances, vesting schedules, dilution math, an exit waterfall. That is arithmetic, and an agent will write it in an afternoon. What you cannot build is a 409A valuation that a board and an auditor will accept, electronic securities issuance that survives legal review, tax paperwork like 83(b) and Rule 701 tracking, or an investor-facing record that your VCs already trust and log into. Cap tables are legal records of who owns your company, and the whole point is that a neutral third party maintains them with an audit trail. A personal build here is a modeling tool, not a system of record.
coreLoopDIY: A local cap table model that records share classes, grants and vesting, then computes fully diluted ownership, dilution from a new round, and an exit waterfall across preferences.
requirements: Willingness to keep the real cap table somewhere your lawyers and investors accept
whatYouLose: 409A valuations with defensible methodology and audit support
Legally sound electronic issuance and signature of securities
Stakeholder and investor portals your cap table is expected to live in
Compliance tracking: 83(b) filings, Rule 701, ISO limits, tax forms
Fund administration, LP reporting and the diligence trail buyers ask for in an acquisition
moatNotes: A cap table is only useful if everyone else agrees it is the cap table. That agreement is the product.
whyPeopleStillPay: Founders do not pay Carta for the math, they pay so that the ownership record is maintained by a party their lawyers, auditors, acquirers and investors already accept without argument. A 409A that survives audit, correctly issued electronic securities, and clean diligence during an acquisition are worth far more than the subscription, and a homemade spreadsheet that quietly miscounts an option pool is a genuinely expensive mistake. The modeling tool is free to build; the trust is not for sale.
notes: Build the waterfall model, keep the system of record where your counsel put it. The moat is not software, it is being the neutral party that auditors, acquirers and every VC on your board already accept.
prompt:
Build a local cap table modeling tool. It is a modeling and scenario tool, explicitly NOT a system of record for securities.

Stack: Vite + React + TypeScript, Tailwind for styling, no backend. All state persists to a single JSON file the user imports and exports, plus localStorage autosave. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry, no analytics.

Data model:
- Stakeholders: name, type (founder, employee, investor, entity).
- Share classes: name, type (common or preferred), liquidation preference multiple, participating or non-participating, participation cap, seniority rank, conversion ratio.
- Issuances: stakeholder, share class, share count, price per share, issue date.
- Option grants: stakeholder, shares, strike price, grant date, vesting (cliff months, total months, monthly or quarterly), exercised amount.
- Option pool: authorized but unissued reserve.
- Convertibles: SAFEs and notes with valuation cap, discount, pre or post money flag, principal, interest rate.

Features:
1. Editable tables for each entity above, with validation and inline errors.
2. Cap table summary: outstanding, fully diluted, ownership percentage per stakeholder, as of a chosen date so vesting is computed correctly.
3. New round modeling: enter pre-money valuation, raise amount, target post-round option pool. Show pre and post ownership, price per share, dilution per stakeholder, and SAFE or note conversion.
4. Exit waterfall: enter an exit value, distribute across preferences by seniority, handle participating and capped participation, decide convert-to-common versus take-preference per class, show payout and effective per-share value for every stakeholder. Show a payout curve chart across a range of exit values.
5. Vesting schedule view per grant with a monthly table.

Out of scope, and say so in the UI footer: 409A valuations, share certificate issuance, e-signature, 83(b) or Rule 701 or tax filings, investor portals, multi-user access.

Include a seed dataset (two founders, a seed SAFE, a Series A, one option pool) so the app is useful on first load. Write a README covering the waterfall assumptions and the rounding rules used. Unit test the waterfall and vesting math with Vitest.
